module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 473

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/473](https://www.erdosproblems.com/473)
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial
  number theory*, Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos473

/--
Is there a permutation $a_1, a_2, \ldots$ of the positive integers such that $a_k + a_{k+1}$ is
always prime?

A question of Segal [ErGr80, p.94]. The answer is yes, as shown by Odlyzko. The linked formal
proof (Codex and GPT-5.6 Sol) builds the permutation as a spanning one-way ray of the graph on the
positive integers in which two numbers are adjacent when their sum is prime.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
  "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/8822f7ddef30fadbd92e1c6ab4ed897af356af5e/src/latest/ErdosProblems/Erdos473.lean#L236"]
theorem erdos_473 : answer(True) ↔
    ∃ a : ℕ ≃ ℕ+, ∀ n : ℕ, ((a n : ℕ) + (a (n + 1) : ℕ)).Prime := by
  sorry

/--
Segal also asked whether for every $n \ge 2$ there is a permutation $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ of
$\{1, \ldots, n\}$ such that $a_k + a_{k+1}$ is prime for all $1 \le k < n$. This is conjectured to
be true, and has been verified for infinitely many $n$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_473.variants.finite : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ n : ℕ, 2 ≤ n → ∃ a : Fin n ≃ Fin n, ∀ k : Fin n, ∀ h : k.val + 1 < n,
      ((a k).val + 1 + ((a ⟨k.val + 1, h⟩).val + 1)).Prime := by
  sorry

end Erdos473

reformulations.difference: The infinite permutation is encoded as a bijection ℕ ≃ ℕ+, with positions indexed from zero rather than one.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Given the Lean bijection a, define the positive-indexed permutation b(k) = a(k − 1). Conversely, set a(n) = b(n + 1). These transformations preserve bijectivity and identify every consecutive pair. The equivalence was proved as infinite_index_shift in /workspace/review/equivalences.lean.

reformulations.difference: A permutation of {1,…,n} is represented by Fin n ≃ Fin n, with one added to each output value and the successor restricted by k.val + 1 < n.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Conjugating by the bijection s(k) = k.val + 1 from Fin n to {1,…,n} produces precisely the source's permutation. The index k corresponds to source position k.val + 1, so the guard selects exactly the pairs with 1 ≤ j < n, without a wraparound edge. This equivalence was proved for every n as finite_index_shift in /workspace/review/equivalences.lean.

sources_consulted: Erdős–Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory (1980), p. 94; https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf
https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/ (bibliography used to locate the book)
https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/Erdos.html (bibliography entry for the cited book)
review.notes: Both declarations are faithful. The source records Odlyzko's affirmative solution of the infinite problem and still describes the finite version as conjectural. The book confirms that the finite question is non-cyclic; the linked MathOverflow discussion concerns a stronger circular variant. Lean checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean and /workspace/review/equivalences.lean compile successfully, including finite witnesses for sizes 0–6 and checks that arbitrary permutations need not satisfy the prime-sum condition. The cited external proof ends with exactly the infinite theorem's right-hand side; it was inspected, not rebuilt. Direct access to the problem page was blocked, so its text was read through Jina and its mathematical wording checked against the book.
